item.title: NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell
item.description:
NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell

NVIDIA announced Sentry, a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Sentry is part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture unveiled at GTC Berlin and runs on NVIDIA BlueField‑4 DPUs.

🔍 Overview

  • Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and stays within defined operational boundaries.
  • It provides host‑isolated runtime protection, controlling the agent’s only path to the model and offering tamper‑evident traceability of agent activity.
  • The framework works even when host resources cannot be trusted, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain.

🧩 How it works

  • Built on NVIDIA DOCA and deployed on BlueField‑4 DPUs, Sentry sits on the node’s sole path to the model and to the outside world.
  • Agent‑to‑model communications are inspected out‑of‑band; Sentry does not rely on the agent to report its own behavior.
  • Real‑time situational awareness is achieved through out‑of‑band observability, continuously evaluating runtime security and behavior.
  • Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment (e.g., container or microVM) to detect external threats and misbehavior.

⚙️ Key components

Component Role
BlueField‑4 DPU Executes Sentry in an isolated trust domain, intercepting all agent traffic before it reaches the host or model.
DOCA Flow Implements a layer‑4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon, blocking unauthorized destinations.
DOCA Tower Transparent proxy built on Envoy; performs layer‑7 inspection, authorization, and TLS termination with in‑silicon acceleration.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) Evaluates access requests against defined policies using the Rego language; runs locally in memory with sub‑millisecond latency.
DOCA Argus Provides live memory introspection of the host, mapping containers, microVMs, processes, threads, and resource relationships to give Sentry contextual evidence.

📡 Network protection

  • Layer‑4 firewall (DOCA Flow) blocks connections to unauthorized destinations.
  • Permitted traffic is forwarded to DOCA Tower for layer‑7 inspection and additional security checks.
  • DOCA Tower terminates TLS using built‑in silicon acceleration, ensuring encrypted traffic is inspected safely.
  • All network traffic reaches BlueField‑4 via a direct I/O path that bypasses host OS and hypervisor packet processing.
  • Policy evaluation is performed by OPA, which can decide on requests in under a millisecond.

📈 Runtime monitoring

  • Out‑of‑band observability continuously evaluates agent behavior for security and integrity.
  • Memory introspection supplies context about containers, microVMs, and other execution environments.
  • DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing volatile host memory on BlueField‑4 and remaining beyond the reach of compromised host software.
  • Argus maps relationships between processes, threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, and memory.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enforces access policies independently of host software, preventing a compromised host or agent from altering restrictions.
  • Provides tamper‑evident traceability of every agent action, helping detect policy violations.
  • Operates in a separate hardware trust domain, keeping security controls out of the agent’s reach.
  • Supports granular, silicon‑level controls on model and tool access, reducing the attack surface for long‑running autonomous agents.
  • Extends OpenShell’s governance model with hardware‑level safeguards, aligning runtime enforcement with infrastructure security.

#NVIDIA #AIsecurity #OpenShell #DPUs

Source: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime | NVIDIA Technical Blog Source: How NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture Secures and Governs AI Agent Workloads at Scale | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS
item.description:
Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS

Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations, but MCP has no built-in authentication standard. This post shows how to fill that gap using Keyfactor EJBCA together with AWS services.

🔍 Overview

  • Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources.
  • MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations.
  • MCP has no built‑in authentication standard.

🛠️ Architecture

The solution combines Keyfactor EJBCA with several AWS managed services and implements three authentication layers that protect each trust boundary in the agent communication chain.

AWS Service Role in the architecture
Amazon Bedrock (via Strands Agents SDK) LLM inference for agents
Amazon RDS for MySQL Application database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets Manager Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2 Hosts Keycloak identity provider and EJBCA PKI server

🔐 Authentication Layers

  1. Layer 1 – User Auth (User → System)
    • Uses OAuth together with an X.509 certificate and delegation minting.
    • Provides user identity and credential binding.
  2. Layer 2 – Agent‑to‑Agent (Agent → Agent)
    • Relies on signed request envelopes containing proof‑of‑possession, a nonce, and a timestamp.
    • Guarantees caller identity, request freshness, and prevents replay.
  3. Layer 3 – MCP Auth (Agent → Tool Server)
    • Combines a scoped token, the signed envelope, and a delegation assertion.
    • Covers all identities, creates a full authorization chain, and incorporates OCSP validation.

⚙️ Key Components & Controls

  • Signed request envelopes – give cryptographic proof‑of‑possession on every agent call.
  • User‑signed delegation assertions – authorize agents without sharing credentials.
  • RFC 8693 audience‑scoped tokens – limit exposure if a token is disclosed.
  • Real‑time OCSP revocation checking – propagates credential changes instantly across agents.
  • EJBCA Enterprise – a PKI platform that supports high‑availability deployment, REST API automation, X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management via web console and REST API.
  • Keyfactor – a machine‑identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide.

🚀 Deployment Options

  • EJBCA can be deployed on‑premises, in containers, or on Amazon EC2.
  • Designed for high‑availability and REST API automation to integrate with AWS services.

💡 Why it matters

  • The added layers supply authentication and authorization that MCP originally lacked.
  • Cryptographic proof‑of‑possession, delegations, scoped tokens, and immediate revocation together reduce the risk of credential misuse while preserving the flexibility of multi‑agent AI workflows.

#AIAgents #PKI #AWS #MCP

Source: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Chris White Develops Dark‑Web Search Tools to Combat Human Trafficking
item.description:
Chris White Develops Dark‑Web Search Tools to Combat Human Trafficking

In summer 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at DARPA to test a new data‑analysis approach aimed at preventing violence and protecting troops in Afghanistan. After the program, DARPA asked him to demonstrate the value of his work on the ground. Later, as director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, White helped create dark‑web search tools used to combat human trafficking.

🔍 Overview

  • In summer 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at DARPA to test a new data‑analysis approach aimed at preventing violence and protecting troops in Afghanistan.
  • At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work on the ground.
  • As director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, White helped create dark‑web search tools used to combat human trafficking.

🛠️ Development and Role

  • Served as on‑the‑ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan.
  • Became a DARPA program manager.
  • Leads the newly formed Cat Lab (Catalyst Lab) in Microsoft Research.
  • Focuses on technology with immediate, real‑world implications.

🏆 Recognition

  • Work featured in Popular Science.
  • Received the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons.

👤 Personal background

  • Harvard postdoc.
  • Nerdy Eagle Scout who built his own computers and hosted LAN parties.
  • Enjoys nature, camping, rock climbing, and debate.

#DARPA #MicrosoftResearch #HumanTrafficking #AI

Source: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact - Microsoft Research

item.title: AI Productivity Surge in Software Development Marks Onset of Singularity
item.description:
AI Productivity Surge in Software Development Marks Onset of Singularity

AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers. A speech delivered on 17 October at an IMF meeting in Bangkok argued that this marks the beginning of the singularity.

🔍 Overview

  • The speaker has spent almost 40 years in journalism and AI research before delivering the talk.
  • The claim is that “the singularity is here” and that this year we have “gained convincing evidence that it has now begun.”
  • The forecast for a singularity was first made by Vernor Vinge in 1993.

📈 Evidence of Productivity Surge

  • “We’ve seen concrete evidence of this inside Anthropic, where our researchers now produce almost 10 times the amount of code than they did for the first four years of the company’s life.”
  • The speaker notes that “AI is now changing national security, it is altering the economic trajectory of the world … and is contributing to its own development.”

🤖 AI in Software Development

  • “We’ve now built AI systems which have been able to augment, extend, and automate aspects of human labor.”
  • “This has most obviously happened in software development, where AI systems are now more capable and efficient than the vast majority of the world’s software engineers.”
  • “As a consequence, the field of software development is changing – A single person is now able to write software for anything they can imagine, creating things that previously would have taken entire teams of humans.”

🌍 Wider Implications

  • AI‑driven scientific invention is expected to “change the course of the global economy, alter the ways countries plan and build their own infrastructure, make us all healthier and able to spend more time with our loved ones.”
  • The most important implication, according to the speaker, is that “in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI, but science as a whole, will speed up.”

⚠️ New Challenges

  • The coding improvements have led to “AI systems have got much better at cybersecurity and cyberattacks –– leading the world to race to deploy these pow…”.
  • For the last half century, “most countries have dealt with falling research productivity while researcher headcount grows rapidly – ideas and inventions appear to be getting harder to find.”
  • The speaker cautions that “AI is on a course to bring about even more change than what we are expecting and we should prepare accordingly.”

#AI #SoftwareEngineering #Singularity #Productivity

Source: Import AI 477: In which I tell the IMF the Singularity has begun

item.title: AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents
item.description:
AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents

AWS is extending its long‑standing Defense‑in‑Depth discipline to AI agents with a new “Trust in Depth” framework.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents can take different execution paths each time they run. (“Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time.”)
  • Traditional safety relies on a human in the loop approving everything the agent does. (“The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does.”)
  • That approach works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. (“That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in.”)
  • People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. (“People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter.”)
  • Caution becomes a bottleneck, leaving capable agents idle on valuable work. (“Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.”)

🛡️ Trust in Depth Concept

  • AWS calls the new layered discipline “Trust in Depth.” (“AWS calls it Trust in Depth.”)
  • It repurposes the industry’s two‑decade‑old Defense in Depth model, which limits what can go wrong, to expand what can be safely allowed. (“Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow.”)
  • The framework consists of four stages:
    • Scope – define the agent’s purpose, required capabilities, and absolute prohibitions before it runs. (“Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?”)
    • Know – record who authorized the agent, its identity, and ensure every acting agent is accounted for at deployment. (“Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?”)
    • Bound – enforce that actions stay within set limits while the agent runs and verify it can still do the job. (“Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?”)
    • Observe – reconstruct the agent’s behavior after each run to enable learning. (“Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?”)

🤖 Automated Reasoning

  • Automated reasoning is mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. (“The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case.”)
  • It can produce a proof that a rule holds on every path described by a precise system model, or pinpoint the exact case where it fails. (“It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof.”)
  • The proof is only as good as the underlying rules and assumptions, making the design work before deployment the hardest part. (“It is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.”)
  • AWS has used automated reasoning in production for over a decade on services such as IAM (handling more than 2.1 billion requests per second), the Nitro Hypervisor, S3 Block Public Access, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer. (“AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents.”)

🛠️ Kiro – Building Agents with Rigor

  • Kiro is an agentic coding system that applies structured, spec‑driven requirements before any code is written. (“Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high‑level intent into structured, spec‑driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written.”)
  • When a rule can be proven, the agent may act autonomously; when proof does not apply, the framework limits the agent’s access and escalates ambiguous cases to a human. (“Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment.”)

💡 Why It Matters

  • As agents handle higher‑stakes work such as financial transactions, a single mistake can be increasingly harmful. (“As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful.”)
  • Organizations need confidence that an AI agent will stay within defined limits even when no one is watching. (“Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching.”)
  • Traditional safeguards—content filtering, testing, and monitoring—are each necessary but none alone can guarantee correct future behavior. (“Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs.”)
  • By combining scoped intent, identity tracking, runtime bounds, post‑run observation, and automated reasoning, Trust in Depth provides a repeatable, auditable safety net for AI agents.

#AWS #AIAgents #AutomatedReasoning #TrustInDepth

Source: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Anthropic Cuts Distillation Attacks by Up to 99% with New Anti‑Distillation Defenses
item.description:
Anthropic Cuts Distillation Attacks by Up to 99% with New Anti‑Distillation Defenses

Anthropic announced that its new anti‑distillation defenses have lowered the amount of reasoning tokens that can be harvested from its Claude models by a factor of 10 to 100, while also reducing the overall effectiveness of distillation attacks by 90‑99%.

🔍 Overview

  • New measures reduce reasoning‑token extraction by 10‑100×.
  • Effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude models lowered by 90‑99%.
  • The company notes there are trade‑offs for legitimate users.

🧩 How Distillation Attacks Work

  • Distillation attacks operate at industrial scale.
  • Attackers build networks of fraudulent accounts to harvest millions of model responses, especially reasoning transcripts that reveal how a model reaches its answers.
  • Harvested data is used to train smaller models that mimic the larger model at a fraction of development cost.
  • Example: Zhipu’s GLM‑5.3 distilled cyber capabilities from leading U.S. models, including Claude, and was judged the most cyber‑capable open‑weights model released to date.
  • Anthropic found its safeguards previously easily bypassed, with models able to develop security exploits end‑to‑end.
  • A reported case involved Moonshot’s Kimi requests being secretly forwarded to Claude for distillation, including a request from a user believed to be linked to China’s People’s Liberation Army analyzing CCTV footage.

⚙️ New Anti‑Distillation Measures

  • Preserved thinking introduced with Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 prevents new API accounts from editing Claude’s prior context, blocking proxy networks from repeatedly extracting protected reasoning.
  • The measure also stops weaker earlier models from reading the reasoning and limits transcript access to the originating organization.
  • A classifier running on Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5 & 5.5, Claude Fable 5 & 5.1 provides robustness comparable to bioweapon‑prevention safeguards, with a false‑positive rate below 0.1%.
  • Persistent distillation attempts trigger account bans, typically within two hours of campaign initiation.
  • Since September 24, Anthropic has resumed charging for requests blocked by safeguards in the sub‑0.1% false‑positive regime.
  • The company has banned tens of thousands of accounts linked to distillation.
  • Developers needed to update integrations to accommodate preserved thinking.
  • The classifier misidentifies benign requests in fewer than 0.1% of cases.
  • Users now pay for blocked requests in protected categories.
Model Role
Claude Sonnet 5.5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Opus 5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Opus 5.5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Fable 5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Fable 5.1 Runs anti‑distillation classifier

📉 Impact

  • After full implementation, reasoning tokens extracted by distillers fell by a factor of 10‑100; on some days the volume was too low to measure.
  • Anthropic states it has turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens of paying traffic from distillers.
  • The defenses achieve a false‑positive rate below 0.1%, matching the robustness of the strongest existing safeguards.

🚀 Outlook

  • Anthropic writes: “We expect that distillation will remain a cat‑and‑mouse game.”
  • The company adds: “We’ll need to continue iterating on our defenses over time.”
  • Platforms can further slow distillation by quickly detecting abuse and off‑boarding fraudulent accounts.

Related Anthropic research includes experiments suggesting small AI models may be months away from self‑replicating on commercial IoT devices, and a report on unintended model actions observed during evaluations.

#Anthropic #AISafety #Distillation #MachineLearning

Source: Anthropic cuts distillation attacks by up to 99% with new defenses

item.title: Google Releases SynthID Detector; Microsoft Teams to Add Deepfake Detection
item.description:
Google Releases SynthID Detector; Microsoft Teams to Add Deepfake Detection

Google has made its SynthID Detector available to the public, and Microsoft announced that Teams will support third‑party deep‑fake detection beginning in November.

🔍 Overview

  • Google opened SynthID Detector to the public.
  • Microsoft Teams will support third‑party deep‑fake detection, expected in November.

⚙️ Key details

  • SynthID Detector is a tool that identifies synthetic media; it is now publicly accessible.
  • Teams integration will allow users to leverage external deep‑fake detection services.

📅 Availability

  • Google’s SynthID Detector: currently public.
  • Microsoft Teams deep‑fake detection: slated for November.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides organizations and individuals with means to verify authenticity of audio/video content.
  • Addresses growing concerns about AI‑generated deepfakes used in misinformation and legal contexts.

#AI #deepfake #privacy #Microsoft #Google

Source: Weekly Letter to Our EDRM Global Community – 13 October 2026

item.title: REA: AI‑Powered Reverse Engineering Across Binaries and Apps
item.description:
REA: AI‑Powered Reverse Engineering Across Binaries and Apps

Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries. REA provides a single MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior.

🔍 Overview

  • “Reverse engineer anything with agents, from app behavior down to native binaries.”
  • “One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior.”
  • “Your agent calls REA through MCP to inspect the target and trace relevant code.”
  • “REA returns findings with their evidence.”

🧩 How it works

  1. Choose your agents – supported agents include Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents.
  2. Setup registers REA with your agent and installs matching workflow instructions.
  3. Setup adds REA’s MCP server and matching workflow instructions, with backups of existing configuration.
  4. Restart your agent afterward.
  5. The agent calls REA through the MCP, which inspects the target and traces relevant code, returning findings with evidence.

⚙️ Key details

  • “Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build and other agents.”
  • “Native analysis can use an existing Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA installation; setup can optionally install Hopper with approval.”
  • “Static JavaScript analysis needs no native analysis engine.”
  • “For native analysis, configure a provider first.”
  • “See the CLI and Evidence guide for native commands, provider selection, snapshots and scripting.”
  • “REA changes quickly, and new releases include frequent bug fixes.”
  • “Keep your installation up to date.”
  • “Bun global updates require Bun 1.2.17 or later.”
  • “With an older Bun release, upgrade Bun manually before running rea update.”
  • “To refresh your agent registrations and skill, run the setup command printed by the update.”
  • “Review the setup changes and restart your agent.”
  • “For one‑off CLI commands, use npx rea-agents@latest followed by the command.”
  • “With Bun, use bunx rea-agents@latest in place of npx rea-agents@latest.”

Supported agents

Supported Agent Status
Claude Code Supported
Codex Supported
Cursor Supported
Gemini CLI Supported
Grok Build Supported
other agents Supported

🚀 Availability

  • “Visit the REA website for setup instructions, illustrated guides, and real case studies.”
  • “See installation and setup for provider configuration and manual MCP registration.”
  • “For native analysis, configure a provider first.”
  • “Replace the path with your target, such as D:/apps/example on Windows.”
  • “Replace Notes with your target app and the feature you want to understand.”
  • “The result includes modules, imports, Electron boundaries and their evidence.”

💡 Why it matters

  • Enables developers and security researchers to understand how a feature works, down to the binary level, using familiar analysis tools and AI agents.
  • Streamlines the workflow from agent selection to evidence generation, reducing manual setup and configuration effort.

#ReverseEngineering #AIAgents #MCP #SoftwareAnalysis

Source: morluto/rea

item.title: Google pushes Android 17 developer preview with battery and privacy enhancements
item.description:
Google pushes Android 17 developer preview with battery and privacy enhancements

The Android ecosystem is busy this weekend as Google released a fresh update to the Android 17 developer preview, focusing on better battery life, background‑process control, and new privacy tweaks.

🔍 Overview

  • Android 17 developer preview arrives with a revamped battery settings menu.
  • Users can now see which background services consume the most power.
  • A new Private Space folder lets you hide specific apps from the app drawer without uninstalling them.
  • Notification snooze lets you silence alerts for one or two hours.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Battery Management
    • Revamped battery settings menu.
    • Visibility of power‑hungry background services.
  • App Privacy
    • Hide apps in the Private Space folder.
    • Google aims to help users find apps that behave badly.
  • Notification Control
    • Swipe a notification to the side for a snooze option.

📱 Additional Android Updates

  • Google Maps – Minor update adds the ability to save multiple custom routes as home‑screen shortcuts.
  • Google Photos – Refresh includes a faster search index for quicker object and person searches.
  • Security Patch – October security patch released for all supported Pixel devices, fixing three major flaws that could allow unauthorized media‑file access. Other manufacturers (OnePlus, Motorola) expected to roll it out by mid‑next week.

🚀 Availability

  • The Android 17 preview is now available for developers.
  • Google plans to open the beta to more devices soon.
  • Reminder: Back up your data before installing major system updates; keeping copies of photos and documents is always wise.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Improved battery visibility helps users extend device runtime.
  • Enhanced privacy controls give users more granular app management.
  • Faster search in Google Photos and custom route shortcuts in Maps streamline everyday tasks.
  • The October security patch addresses critical vulnerabilities, reinforcing device security across the ecosystem.

#android #android17 #mobileupdates #privacy #security

Source: Android Daily News: October 10, 2026 – Latest Updates and Releases - thetechpapa

item.title: Mattermost hires Senior Mobile Engineer, adds AI agents to boost reliability
item.description:
Mattermost hires Senior Mobile Engineer, adds AI agents to boost reliability

Mattermost is seeking a Senior Mobile Engineer to own reliability, performance, and platform evolution for its React Native and TypeScript mobile application, including native iOS and Android integrations.

🔍 Overview

  • “Mattermost is the leading collaborative workflow platform for defense, intelligence, security, and critical infrastructure.”
  • “Trusted by the U.S. Department of War and Fortune 500s, our platform runs on‑premises and in private clouds, delivering secure messaging, file sharing, workflow automation, audio/screenshare, and project management—all with full data and operational control.”
  • “Mattermost powers high‑stakes workflows across mission planning, real‑time, real‑world operations, DevSecOps, incident response, and cyber defense—enabling secure collaboration from tactical edge and DDIL environments to enterprise HQ.”
  • “Teams operate across web, desktop, and mobile, with embedded interoperability for Microsoft Teams, Outlook, and Microsoft 365.”

🎯 Role & Responsibilities

  • “The role focuses on building resilient offline‑capable behavior for disconnected, denied, intermittent, and limited‑connectivity environments used by defense and critical‑infrastructure teams.”
  • “The engineer will diagnose production issues using telemetry, device profiling, crash data, native traces, and limited field logs while improving synchronization, storage, rendering, networking, and battery performance.”
  • “This is a senior hands‑on ownership role that includes architecture decisions, mentoring, security‑conscious engineering, and collaboration with platform, feature, and customer‑facing teams.”
  • “U.S. federal and export‑control eligibility requirements apply, and the role may require obtaining a U.S. government security clearance.”
  • “Your immediate focus will be making that experience more reliable and performant.”
  • “Over time, you’ll also help shape the next generation of our cross‑platform mobile architecture.”
  • “You’ll work hands‑on across application and native layers, partner closely with platform and feature teams, work directly with customer‑facing teams on field reports from constrained environments, and help raise the bar for how we observe, diagnose, and build mobile software.”

🤖 AI‑Assisted Development

  • “I would use agents to accelerate bounded tasks such as test generation, code exploration, refactoring proposals, and documentation, while keeping design decisions and security review under human ownership.”
  • “Generated changes should pass normal code review, static analysis, dependency scrutiny, device testing, and reliability validation, especially around authentication, secure storage, networking, and native APIs.”

🛠 Technical Approach

  • “I would use a local‑first model with durable on‑device storage, an explicit operation queue, idempotent requests, retry backoff, and conflict‑resolution rules.”
  • “I would model connectivity as a changing state rather than a binary signal, preserve user intent locally, and expose clear sync status so the application remains predictable during recovery.”
  • “I would first segment crash data by app version, OS version, device model, affected code path, and rollout cohort to identify the highest‑impact signature.”
  • “I would correlate crash traces with release changes and telemetry, reproduce on representative physical devices where possible, ship a focused mitigation or rollback, and then add monitoring or tests to prevent recurrence.”
  • “I would establish baselines using device profiling and production metrics, then identify costly initialization, bridge traffic, large synchronous storage reads, unnecessary renders, and oversized assets.”
  • “Improvements could include deferred initialization, optimized state hydration, native‑side work for platform‑specific hot paths, render profiling, and validation against startup, memory, and battery regression budgets.”
  • “I separate urgent containment work from strategic platform investment and explain the operational risk, expected impact, and delivery cost of each option.”
  • “I favor incremental seams that solve a present failure mode while moving the codebase toward a clearer long‑term architecture, supported by measurable reliability and performance outcomes.”

📋 Application Steps

  • “Review the role, location requirements, compensation details, and application process before deciding whether this opportunity fits your next career move.”
  • “Prepare your resume, explore your fit, and draft a cover letter for this opportunity.”
  • “Make your next move.”
  • “To learn more, visit www.mattermost.com”

#Mattermost #MobileEngineering #AIagents #Security

Source: Remote Senior Mobile Engineer at Mattermost - Jobicy

item.title: China Telecom’s TeleAgent reaches 1.5 million users and launches private‑deployment edition
item.description:
China Telecom’s TeleAgent reaches 1.5 million users and launches private‑deployment edition

China Telecom’s office AI agent, TeleAgent, announced that it has grown to 1.5 million registered users and over 200,000 daily active users – a sharp rise from just 27,000 registered users in mid‑June. The milestone was revealed by Liu Guiqing at the opening of PT Expo China 2026, after the product’s first unveiling at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference (WAIC) 2026.

🔍 Overview

  • User growth: 1.5 M registered users, >200 K DAU (up from 27 K in mid‑June).\

item.title: AI Models Now Engineered to Refuse Dangerous Requests
item.description:
AI Models Now Engineered to Refuse Dangerous Requests

Today’s large language models (LLMs) are deliberately engineered to disobey dangerous requests, a shift from early systems that would “blab on about anything.”

🔍 Overview

  • In 2021, Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless. They said that when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.
  • Modern LLMs are trained on billions of web pages, giving them a broad mastery of violence and vitriol, but companies now layer refusal mechanisms to curb that knowledge.
  • The goal is to have the model turn down prompts such as how to poison a colleague, how to tie a noose, or how to build autonomous drone swarms.

⚙️ How Refusal Is Implemented

  • Companies run a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing harmful questions and punish it for “over‑refusing” harmless prompts.
  • In many cases other models are used to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no.
  • For additional protection, models are placed behind tranches of other AI that block mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent core.

📊 Effectiveness and Limits

  • “If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down.”
  • Yet, “AI refusal is far from foolproof—and could become an instrument of repression.”
  • The mechanisms are probabilistic, so they are “never likely to be all that reliable.”
  • When refusal fails, the consequences can be severe: “It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results,” and “failed refusals might result in global calamity.”

🚨 Reported Misuse Attempts

  • Companies report users trying to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms with the most advanced AI.
  • “Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to.”
  • Some of the latest models are reported to be “as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, … as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.”

🤔 Open Questions

  • “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, OpenAI board member and co‑founder of Gray Swan.
  • Currently, “AI companies get to draw that line.”
  • The Pentagon has expressed interest in fewer refusals, indicating tension between safety and utility.
  • There is evidence that AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.

📚 Historical Context

  • Early chatbots could easily provide harmful instructions. Ryan McBain (Harvard) recalls that asking “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” could “very easily generate a response.”
  • In 2022, before mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red‑teamers” (including Paul Röttger) to probe the model slated for ChatGPT, with the task to ask any questions they deemed “refusal‑wor…”.
  • These red‑team efforts highlighted how far the technology had to go to reliably refuse dangerous prompts.

(Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)

#AIRefusal #LLMs #Safety #RedTeam

Source: We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no

item.title: Agents Shipgate adds deterministic local‑first tool‑use readiness review
item.description:
Agents Shipgate adds deterministic local‑first tool‑use readiness review

🔍 Overview

Agents Shipgate is an open‑source CLI and GitHub Action that provides a deterministic merge gate for AI‑generated agent capability changes. It performs a local‑first, static Tool‑Use Readiness review of a pull request before the agent receives production‑like permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • The tool runs locally and statically – it does not execute the agent, make tool calls, invoke LLMs, or access the network.
  • It scans a wide range of tool‑surface definitions (MCP, OpenAPI, SDKs, workflow artifacts, etc.) and produces a deterministic Tool‑Use Readiness Report.
  • Using the diff command, it compares the PR branch with its merge base on the repository’s default branch (e.g., origin/main). One entry is printed per changed grant or replaced rule.
  • If the PR targets a non‑default branch, the --base flag can be used (e.g., --base origin/feature).
  • No manifest, policy, saved baseline, skill, or account is required, and nothing is written back to the repository.

⚙️ Key details

  • Open‑source CLI + GitHub Action.
  • Scans the following tool surfaces:
    Tool Surface Included in Scan
    MCP ✅
    OpenAPI ✅
    OpenAI Agents SDK ✅
    Anthropic Messages API ✅
    Google ADK ✅
    LangChain/LangGraph ✅
    CrewAI ✅
    OpenAI API ✅
    Codex repo config ✅
    Codex plugin ✅
    n8n ✅
    Conductor OSS workflow artifacts ✅
  • Shows source‑observed changes per agent, including before/after signatures and source locations, unless a specific --scope is provided.
  • Supports comparison of OpenAI Agents SDK and Google ADK tool bindings without a manifest or baseline.
  • Prints one entry per changed grant; static configuration reflects what files permit, not what the agent actually did.
  • Provides a review question asking whether the declared capability changes are intended.

🚀 Availability

  • The deterministic merge gate functionality is new in version 1.2.0.
  • Install from PyPI into a clean virtual environment (e.g., pipx install agents-shipgate).
  • Users of older releases need to upgrade with pipx upgrade agents-shipgate.
  • Example usage in version 1.2.0 shows three changes from four rows, with three widening what the agent may do.

💡 Why it matters

Agents Shipgate lets developers see exactly what capability changes a coding‑agent PR introduces before it merges. Because the review is performed locally and without network access, teams can safely assess permission changes without executing the agent or contacting external services. This deterministic, static analysis helps enforce intentional tool‑use policies and reduces the risk of unintended privilege expansions.

#AIagents #ToolUseReadiness #OpenSource

Source: ThreeMoonsLab/agents-shipgate

item.title: Keystroke Analysis Detects LLM‑Assisted Vietnamese Writing
item.description:
Keystroke Analysis Detects LLM‑Assisted Vietnamese Writing

A new study submitted on 6 Oct 2026 examines how keystroke dynamics can reveal when large language models (LLMs) assist Vietnamese text production, even when users try to hide their involvement.

🔍 Overview

  • Focuses on the robustness of keystroke‑based detection of LLM‑assisted writing.
  • Introduces a Vietnamese keystroke dataset covering multiple realistic writing modes.
  • Defines a behaviorally grounded threat model where users deliberately alter typing patterns.

🗂️ Dataset

  • Bona fide composition – natural, unaided Vietnamese typing.
  • Transcription – copying text verbatim.
  • Paraphrasing – re‑expressing content while preserving meaning.

⚙️ Threat Model

  • Users create behaviorally manipulated variants of the keystroke data to evade detection.
  • These manipulated samples are used to test the limits of keystroke‑based classifiers.

🤖 Models Evaluated

Model Representation Type
Temporal features Feature‑based
Rhythmic features Feature‑based
1D‑CNN Sequential
TypeNet Sequential
  • Evaluations are performed under user‑independent and context‑independent settings.

📊 Findings

  • Sequential models (1D‑CNN, TypeNet) outperform feature‑based approaches in most scenarios.
  • Keystroke signals contain discriminative information about the writing process.
  • Transcription is reliably identified.
  • Paraphrasing and adversarially manipulated samples are often misclassified as genuine when not explicitly modeled.
  • Applying adversarial training with behaviorally manipulated data markedly improves separability and robustness.

💡 Implications

  • Success of keystroke‑based detection hinges on exposure to a diverse range of writing behaviors.
  • Strong performance in limited conditions does not automatically generalize to realistic or adversarial environments without targeted modeling.

🚀 Community Context

  • The paper is hosted on arXiv, which collaborates with arXivLabs, a framework for developing and sharing new arXiv features while upholding openness, community, excellence, and user‑data privacy.

#keystrokes #LLMDetection #Vietnamese #AdversarialAI

Source: Detecting LLM-Assisted Vietnamese Writing via Keystrokes under Behavioral Manipulation

item.title: Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege
item.description:
Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege

Amazon Quick now offers a reliable way to downgrade user roles using the AWS Command Line Interface, filling a gap where the console does not support direct transitions such as Admin to Reader or Author to Reader.

🔍 Overview

Managing access permissions effectively is an important aspect of maintaining a secure and collaborative environment. Amazon Quick supports versatile user management options for various identity types. You can provision users natively or through enterprise identity providers like AWS IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Regular audits of user roles are recommended to confirm everyone has appropriate permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • Roles are assigned and grouped according to job functions: Admin, Author, and Reader.
  • The principle of least privilege applies strongly to administration; downgrading roles is a key part of enforcing it.
  • For more granular control, consider Custom Permissions, which restrict capabilities within a role tier.
  • Integration with AWS IAM adds permission boundaries beyond the built-in role system.

⚙️ Key details

  • The console does not provide direct downgrade paths for all transitions (e.g., Admin to Reader or Author to Reader).
  • The update-user API also rejects direct downgrades with a “You cannot downgrade a user role” error.
  • Two reliable solutions exist: manual deletion-and-recreation and a CLI method.
  • The CLI step-down method works for legacy BI-only roles: Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader.
  • The same sequence works for Pro users when intermediate steps use legacy roles (e.g., Author Pro > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader Pro).
  • Before downgrading, verify that users are currently Admin or Author. Downgraded users lose ability to edit resources they previously owned.
  • For large organizations, the CLI method can load user email addresses from a CSV file.
  • AWS CloudShell can be used without specifying the AWS Region, as it uses the current console context.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Quick offers two subscription tiers with distinct role sets:

Subscription Roles Features
Amazon Quick Enterprise Admin Pro, Author Pro, Reader Pro Full BI + AI features (agents, topics, Q&A, stories, generative summaries)
Amazon Quick Sight (BI-only) Admin, Author, Reader Traditional BI authoring and consumption

Prerequisites include an active AWS account with administrator access to Amazon Quick, and the AWS CLI installed and configured if using the CLI method.

💡 Why it matters

  • Role-based pricing means Authors and Admins pay a fixed monthly per-user fee, while Readers use session-based pricing—downgrading can reduce costs.
  • Downgrading helps enforce least privilege, a practice recommended in the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
  • Proactively transferring ownership of dashboards and analyses when responsibilities change prevents orphaned resources and maintains business continuity.

#AWS #QuickSight #UserManagement #IAM #Security

Source: Downgrading user roles in Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds JWT-secured Claude Desktop web-search integration
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds JWT-secured Claude Desktop web-search integration

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now supports a secure integration that lets Claude Desktop invoke a fully managed web‑search tool via the AgentCore Gateway.

🔍 Overview

  • AgentCore: a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model.
  • AgentCore Gateway: a capability of AgentCore that can close the knowledge‑cutoff gap by connecting Claude Desktop to Web Search.
  • Web Search: a fully managed, Model Context Protocol (MCP)‑compatible search service backed by an Amazon index of tens of billions of documents.
  • All query traffic stays within AWS infrastructure, with no external API keys and no queries leaving your boundary.

🧩 How it works

  1. IAM Identity Center authenticates the user via SAML.
  2. Amazon Cognito is registered as a federation layer; it receives the SAML assertion and issues a JSON Web Token (JWT).
  3. Claude Desktop uses an app client (with client secret) to start the OAuth 2.0 authorization‑code flow, obtains the JWT, and calls the AgentCore Gateway.
  4. The AgentCore Gateway validates the JWT on each request and forwards the query to the Web Search target.
  5. The entire authentication chain stays within AWS.

⚙️ Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permissions to create IAM roles and Bedrock AgentCore resources.
  • Admin access in the AWS Organizations management account for IAM Identity Center configuration.
  • AWS IAM Identity Center pre‑configured for SSO access to AWS accounts.
  • Claude Desktop set up with Amazon Bedrock as the inference provider.
  • AWS CLI v2 installed and configured.
  • Python 3.10 or later.
  • Latest Boto3 SDK.

🛠️ Setup steps

  1. Verify the target region is us-east-1, eu-west-1, or ap-northeast-1 (the only regions where Web Search on AgentCore is available).
  2. In the target AWS account, create an Amazon Cognito user pool to act as the OpenID Connect (OIDC) token issuer.
  3. In the AWS Organizations management account, create a SAML application that federates with Cognito and assign the users or groups that should access Web Search.
  4. Back in the target account, register IAM Identity Center as a SAML identity provider in the Cognito user pool.
  5. Create a Cognito app client with a client secret; Claude Desktop will use this client to initiate the OAuth flow.
  6. Create a new AgentCore Gateway, set Inbound Auth Type to JSON Web Tokens (JWT), and enable the Web Search tool.
  7. Claude Desktop connects to the AgentCore Gateway using the JWT obtained from Cognito.

🚀 Availability

Region Identifier
US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1
Europe (Ireland) eu-west-1
Asia Pacific (Tokyo) ap-northeast-1

💡 Why it matters

  • Enterprises can keep all search queries inside their AWS boundary, eliminating the need to manage external API keys.
  • The JWT‑based inbound authentication leverages existing SSO (IAM Identity Center) and federation (Cognito) services, simplifying access control.
  • The integration provides a practical way to reduce the knowledge‑cutoff limitation of Claude Desktop by tapping a live web index.

#AmazonBedrock #AIAgents #WebSearch #AWSSecurity

Source: Add secure Web Search to Claude Desktop with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services

item.title: US Government Requests $30.3 Million for AI-Powered Polygraph Modernization
item.description:
US Government Requests $30.3 Million for AI-Powered Polygraph Modernization

The US government has requested $30.3 million over the next five years to develop an improved form of lie detector known as Polygraph+ (or Polygraph Next). The program aims to modernize federal credibility assessment technologies to enhance accuracy and reliability.

🔍 Overview

Managed by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA), Polygraph+ will be utilized for the vetting of prospective employees and “insider threat detection.” This comes as the Pentagon has increasingly used polygraph tests under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to identify sources of press leaks, including the testing of approximately 50 Joint Staff officers following reports on US weapons stockpiles in the war with Iran.

🧩 How it works

The program focuses on two primary technical advancements:

  • AI and Machine Learning: The use of scoring algorithms to find patterns in data that human examiners may miss and to create “multi-modal” deception detection by combining multiple measurements into a single score.
  • Standoff Sensing: The ability to take physiological readings without attaching a device to the subject.

⚙️ Key details

Following an open submission process by the Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) in 2023, two companies were selected to build prototypes:

Company Capability/Focus
Presage Technologies Measuring heart rate and breathing rate using standard cameras
Altec Research Non-contact sensing tracking head movement, facial skin temperature, and pore activity

💡 Why it matters

Current polygraph technology, largely unchanged since the 1920s, relies on measurements of sweat, breathing, pulse, and blood pressure. However, the technology faces significant criticism:

  • Reliability Issues: In 1983, Congress’s Office of Technology Assessment found limited evidence supporting its use for employee screening, and in 2003, the US National Research Council called the evidence for its efficacy “weak at best.”
  • Subjectivity and Bias: Interpretations can vary wildly between examiners, and individuals from minority groups are more likely to be judged as deceptive.
  • Countermeasures: Interviewees can beat the test through training, such as using a pin in a shoe to artificially heighten physiological responses.
  • Scale Risks: With 2.8 million employees in the DOD, an imperfect system could result in tens of thousands of false accusations.

Critics such as legal scholar Kyri Kotsoglou describe the effort as “a misguided effort to reduce the complex to something that is tangible,” while associate professor Sophie van der Zee notes that while various strategies like brain scans and thermal cameras have been tried, “There is still no Pinocchio’s nose.”

#AI #MachineLearning #Defense #Polygraph #Biometrics

Source: The Pentagon wants $30 million to build an AI-powered lie detector

item.title: AWS Labs releases TOLAP: Open‑source tool‑object level access control
item.description:
AWS Labs releases TOLAP: Open‑source tool‑object level access control

TOLAP (Tool‑Object Level Access Protocol) is now available as an open‑source project under Apache‑2.0. It provides a specification and libraries that let teams enforce fine‑grained access policies at the data source.

🔍 Overview

  • “Tool‑Object Level Access Protocol (TOLAP) closes that gap.”
  • Role‑based access control answers whether a user can reach a resource, while attribute‑based access control evaluates policy at a centralized engine.
  • Database row‑level security is genuinely enforcement at the source — and it’s worth using.
  • Guardrails constrain what the model says, and agent frameworks such as Amazon Bedrock Agents, Azure AI Agent Service, Google Vertex AI Agents, and LangChain authorize whether the agent may invoke a tool.

🧩 How it works

  • Policy is applied where the data originates, not in a layer above it.
  • “The tool wraps the data source and enforces before anything crosses the boundary.”
  • Policies name individual data objects — columns, rows, fields, tags, endpoints, HTTP methods, similarity thresholds, storage prefixes, result limits.
  • The calling agent needs no security‑aware code.
  • “Your code fetches the data; TOLAP decides what may leave.”

⚙️ Key details

Component Description
Versioned policy schema Three layers: definition, assignment (links to user or group with scope and expiry), and merged effective policy that actually gets enforced. One schema spans databases, APIs, knowledge bases, and object storage.
Normative specification Defines canonical signing, the enforcement pipeline order, and the fail‑closed rules.
SDKs ( .NET, Python, TypeScript ) Each ships a core, store and enforcement package; core packages have zero external dependencies in all three languages.
Reference policy server & authoring console For teams who’d rather run a policy service than build one.
Integrations Fourteen tested integrations across the three languages, including MCP SDK, Strands, LangChain, LangChain.js, Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, OpenAI Agents, Pydantic AI, Semantic Kernel, and Bedrock Agents.
  • TOLAP is not an MCP server and does not speak the MCP protocol.
  • It provides enforcement around the function your tool layer already calls.

🚀 Availability

  • “Today it’s available as open source under Apache-2.0 at github.com/awslabs/tolap.”
  • The repository contains the five items listed above and fourteen worked integrations with popular agent frameworks.

💡 Why it matters

  • Row‑level security and guardrails are essential for safe AI‑driven applications.
  • Agent frameworks need a way to authorize tool invocations; TOLAP supplies that capability.
  • By delivering a shared specification and ready‑made libraries, “every team doesn’t have to solve it from scratch,” accelerating secure AI development.

#TOLAP #AccessControl #AIAgents #OpenSource

Source: Introducing TOLAP: object-level access control for AI agent tools | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput
item.description:
NVIDIA Blackwell Confidential Computing retains up to 98% LLM inference throughput

NVIDIA demonstrated that running a 32K‑input/1K‑output LLM inference workload inside confidential virtual machines (CVMs) on a Blackwell‑based DGX B200 system keeps almost all of the baseline performance.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA Confidential Computing (CC) provides memory‑encrypted CVMs, confidential GPUs, and encrypted NVLink, enabling LLM inference to run securely while preserving throughput.

🧩 How it works

  • Secure data path – The Blackwell CC architecture enforces hardware‑based protection for data and workloads in use.
  • Host‑to‑device transfer – In the B200 CC, transfers go through a software‑encrypted bounce buffer because the GPU cannot directly access protected CVM memory.
  • TensorRT LLM adaptations
    • Uses CC‑aware memory selection, opting for pageable memory on protected paths instead of always using pinned memory.
    • Moves repeated‑token and sampling‑data readback to an asynchronous worker, so protected copies do not block the main scheduler during decode.
    • Measures tactics with the GPU %globaltimer inside CC while keeping CUDA events outside CC.
  • NVLink limitation – NVLS (NVLink SHARP) multicast is not available in B200 CC configurations.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model: nvidia/DeepSeek-R1-0528-NVFP4
  • Inference framework: TensorRT LLM (Docker container) with PyTorch backend
  • Sequence lengths: 32K input, 1K output
  • Parallelism: TP=8, EP=1, PP=1; KV cache in FP8
  • Concurrency tested: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 requests
  • Hardware: 1 NVIDIA DGX B200 system (8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs), GPU power limit 1,000 W
  • Platform: Intel TDX
  • Host OS / kernel: Ubuntu 25.10 / 6.17.0-20-generic
  • Guest OS / kernel: Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS / 6.8.0-124-generic, 256 vCPUs, 2 NUMA nodes
  • Driver / software stack: NVIDIA driver 595.71.05, VBIOS FW 1.4.x, CUDA 13.2, TensorRT LLM 1.3.0rc22, NCCL v2.30, OpenSSL 3.6.0, Docker + NVIDIA Container Toolkit

📈 Performance results

  • Across concurrency levels 1–16, CC retained 96.1 %–98.2 % of the output‑token throughput compared with a non‑confidential baseline.
  • Mean TPOT (time‑per‑output‑token) stayed within 1.2 %–4.3 % of the baseline.
  • These results show that the security overhead of CC is limited to a few percent while providing full data protection.

💡 Why it matters

The Blackwell confidential computing architecture creates a hardware‑enforced security path that protects data in use without sacrificing most of the inference performance required for large‑scale LLM deployments.

item.title: Website Administrator Deploys Anubis Proof‑of‑Work to Thwart AI Scrapers
item.description:
Website Administrator Deploys Anubis Proof‑of‑Work to Thwart AI Scrapers

The administrator of a website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites.

🔍 Overview

  • Anubis is a protective measure installed by the site admin.
  • It targets AI companies that scrape websites aggressively.

🧩 How it works

  • Employs a Proof‑of‑Work scheme inspired by Hashcash.
  • The work imposes negligible cost on individual users but becomes costly for large‑scale scrapers.

⚙️ Key details

  • Designed as a “good enough” placeholder to buy time for fingerprinting and headless‑browser detection (e.g., via font rendering).
  • Requires modern JavaScript features that are disabled by privacy plugins such as JShelter.
  • Classified as a hack rather than a full‑featured solution.

💡 Why it matters

  • Increases the economic cost of mass scraping, deterring abusive AI scrapers while keeping impact on normal visitors low.
  • Allows site owners to focus resources on more sophisticated bot‑detection techniques.

#Anubis #ProofOfWork #WebScraping #JSPrivacy #BotDetection

Source: Making sure you’re not a bot!
